THE WORLD: METAPHOR WORLDS
A fictional fishing harbour town of about 600 people on a granite headland on a cold North Atlantic coast, in late May, when icebergs drift south past the coast. The town sits around a small sheltered harbour that opens to the east; a white lighthouse stands on the headland south of the harbour mouth, with its keeper's house and a walled kitchen garden in the lee of the tower; behind the town a footpath climbs a bare hill to a summit cairn; across the narrow inlet north of the town a new concrete road bridge is being built from both banks. Every set is a spot in this one place, so the same lighthouse, the same granite and the same sea recur. No real town is drawn.

- the harbour: a straight quay of squared granite blocks with a concrete capping, black cast-iron bollards about 5 m apart and 0.5 m back from the edge, vertical timber fenders on the quay face, a steel ladder recessed into the wall; a curved rubble breakwater of big granite blocks across the south side of the harbour mouth, with a short white light tower with a red lantern on its head, and a small green light on a white post at the quay's end
- single-storey fishing stores along the quay: timber sheds with pitched roofs of dark grey corrugated sheet, wide double doors, weathered silver-grey boards
- the lighthouse: a round tapering tower of white-painted masonry about 18 m tall on the headland's highest rock, a black-painted iron gallery with railings, a glazed lantern with diagonal glazing bars and a red-painted domed roof with a ball vent; inside, below the lantern, a round watch room holds the weight-driven clockwork that still turns the lens; the station is kept as a working heritage light, wound by hand by a part-time keeper
- the land: bare grey-pink granite in rounded outcrops and cliffs, low wind-shaped spruce in the hollows, crowberry and grass heath, small dark ponds; no tall trees
- the new bridge: a concrete box-girder road bridge built by the balanced cantilever method, two slim piers in the inlet, each carrying a deck that grows outward both ways in 5 m segments, with yellow form travellers at the tips of the growing deck and a tower crane beside each pier
Materials: grey-pink granite, painted clapboard (muted ochre, oxblood, slate blue, off-white), silver-grey weathered timber, black cast iron and painted steel, white-painted masonry, fresh pale-grey concrete, rope and netting, a deep blue-green sea and white-and-pale-blue ice; signal red and orange only on things that carry them in life (the lantern roof, the breakwater light, lifebuoys, fishing floats, a rescue boat's collar), and warning yellow only on the bridge's construction plant (the cranes, the form travellers). QUALITY CHECK (run it before you reply; redraw what fails and say what you changed)
Layout:
- Layout is cinematography: the camera height, angle and staging are decided before any rendering. Plan every set as far, mid and near ground, and leave clear space for the characters on the floor and around their heads, with breathing room on the side they will face.
- Prefer a low horizon (seated or standing eye height, never a high bird's-eye) so the room is not mostly empty floor and character sizes read clearly.
- Lead the eye with the architecture (a walkway, a table edge, a row of columns, the light pattern) to one focal point; the squint test must still show that focal point and the free space for the characters.
- Keep the backgrounds' values and patterns apart from where characters will stand: no busy pattern or high-contrast edge behind a head.
- Every receding edge goes to its vanishing point; furniture rotated to the room gets its own vanishing points on the same horizon.
- Parallax: draw the walls and floor complete behind the furniture (no holes when layers slide), run the far layer past the frame edges into the overscan, and keep the near layer to one or two framing objects.
- Cast shadows and contact shadows on everything that touches a surface; without them objects look pasted in.
Real-world sense (nothing absurd):
- The horizon is the one in the camera line; furniture sits ON the floor with contact shadows; nothing floats,
  intersects a wall or passes through another object.
- Sizes agree with the scale list: chairs fit under tables, doors are taller than people, screens and windows are
  the stated sizes, steps and sills are reachable.
- The set was drawn, not modelled: soft things have curved edges, chairs have shaped backs and seats, and no shape is
  an unexplained slab or patch.
- Every object reads at a glance and in silhouette as what it is (a chair as a chair, a plant as a real plant);
  every object listed in the scene is present, and nothing is there that would not be in this place.
- Light has one logic: every cast shadow falls away from the named source at a consistent angle; screens and lamps
  glow only if they are on in this version.
- No people, no letters, numbers or logos; slots are empty rects; the palette is exact.
Not in this style:
- neon on everything
- glow on surfaces with no light source
- outlines
- a muddy dark with no clear light shapes
- night drawn as a darker copy of the day scene
Not in this world:
- real towns, real lighthouses, flags, names on boats or buildings, signs with words, brands or logos
- a tropical or Mediterranean look: palm trees, sandy beaches, terracotta roofs, turquoise water
- a lighthouse with painted stripes, no gallery or a lantern without glazing bars
- icebergs inside the harbour, or an iceberg drawn as a floating white triangle with nothing under the water
- people in the sets (the cast is separate)
- a cartoon-clean place: every set shows that people live and work here
- objects at the wrong size: a person must fit through a door, a bollard reaches only to the knee
Not in this set:
- the two arms already touching (the gap is the point of the main set)
- a suspension or cable-stayed bridge, cables, towers or arches: this is a concrete box girder built by balanced cantilever
- an arm without its pier under it, or a deck that floats
- a crane top or a traveller rising into the sky behind a head
- a guard rail or fence across the foreground that the bridge is seen through
- names, logos or words on the cranes, the travellers or the boat
